key_terms.meaning: A fraction of the output is returned to the input so that it opposes the input; closed-loop gain falls from A to A/(1+Aβ).
The fraction of the output signal returned to the input; a pure ratio (V/V or A/A), no unit.
Open-loop gain A multiplied by β; its size decides how much the feedback changes the amplifier.
A × BW; nearly constant for a single-pole amplifier, so a gain cut of (1+Aβ) widens bandwidth by (1+Aβ).
The feedback signal is added in series with the input voltage; input resistance rises by (1+Aβ).
The feedback signal is added in parallel at the input node; input resistance falls by (1+Aβ).
The output voltage is sensed across the load; output resistance falls by (1+Aβ).
The output current is sensed in series with the load; output resistance rises by (1+Aβ).
PM = 180° − |∠Aβ| measured at the frequency where |Aβ| = 1; 45° to 60° is a safe target.
GM = −20 log₁₀|Aβ| in dB, measured where the loop phase is −180°; positive GM means stable.
For steady oscillation the loop gain Aβ must equal 1∠0° (or a whole multiple of 360°) at one frequency only.
The returned signal adds to the input; gain becomes A/(1−Aβ) and grows without limit as Aβ → 1.
Three RC sections give 180° of shift at one frequency; the amplifier supplies the other 180°.
A lead-lag RC network gives 0° shift at f₀ = 1/(2πRC) and needs an amplifier gain of exactly 3.
f₀ = 1/(2π√(L_eq C_eq)); the tank presents a high impedance and 0° loop phase at f₀.
A tapped inductor gives L_eq = L₁ + L₂ (plus mutual terms) with a single capacitor C.
A capacitor divider C₁, C₂ taps the tank; C_eq = C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂) with a single inductor L.
Colpitts plus a small capacitor C₃ in the inductor branch, so f₀ ≈ 1/(2π√(L C₃)) when C₃ is much smaller than C₁ and C₂.
Quartz turns mechanical strain into voltage and back, so it acts as an electrical resonator.
Q = 2π × (energy stored ÷ energy lost per cycle); quartz reaches tens of thousands, giving very small frequency drift.

takeaways: Negative feedback trades gain for everything else: bandwidth, distortion, impedance control and gain that depends only on β.
The factor (1+Aβ) is the single number that sets how much gain is lost and how much bandwidth and linearity are gained.
Sampling the output voltage lowers output resistance; sampling the output current raises it; series mixing raises input resistance and shunt mixing lowers it.
An amplifier is stable while the loop-gain magnitude falls below 1 before the loop phase reaches −180°; the two margins measure how close it gets.
An oscillator is a positive-feedback amplifier whose loop gain is exactly 1 at one frequency and less than 1 at every other frequency.
Excess loop gain above 1 is what starts oscillation; a nonlinear or temperature-dependent element is what holds the amplitude steady at 1.
RC oscillators suit audio frequencies because resistor and capacitor values stay practical; LC oscillators suit radio frequencies because the tank sets a sharp resonant frequency.
A quartz crystal gives frequency stability in parts per million, which is why clocks, watches and radio transmitters use it.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to derive the closed-loop gain formula, name and justify all four feedback topologies with their impedance effects, sketch a Bode plot and read the margins from it, then apply the Barkhausen criterion to a named oscillator circuit with f₀ and the gain condition worked out numerically.

bank.q: Define negative feedback. Derive the closed-loop gain A_vf = A/(1+Aβ) for a series-shunt amplifier, and explain what the factor (1+Aβ) does to gain, bandwidth and distortion.
outline: Block diagram with summing node, A block and β block
v_f = βv_o, v_i = v_s − v_f, so A_vf = A/(1+Aβ)
Loop gain Aβ defined; β must be a pure ratio
Gain falls by (1+Aβ); bandwidth rises by the same factor, A×BW roughly constant
Distortion and noise generated inside the amplifier fall by (1+Aβ)
Gain depends on β, so it is set by resistors and not by transistor parameters

bank.q: Name the four negative-feedback topologies. For each, state what is sampled at the output, what is mixed at the input, and the effect on input and output resistance.
outline: Two choices on the output: voltage (node) sampling or current (loop) sampling
Two choices at the input: series mixing or shunt mixing
Voltage sampling lowers R_out; current sampling raises R_out
Series mixing raises R_in; shunt mixing lowers R_in
Table of the four combinations: voltage-series, voltage-shunt, current-series, current-shunt
One practical example for each, e.g. emitter follower as voltage-series

bank.q: State the Barkhausen criterion for oscillation. Explain why a practical oscillator needs the loop gain to be slightly more than 1 at the start.
outline: Condition: Aβ = 1 in magnitude and total loop phase = 0° or a whole multiple of 360°
Negative-resistance or positive-feedback view of the circuit
At start no signal exists, so Aβ > 1 lets a small disturbance grow
Amplitude growth stops when the device becomes nonlinear and the average loop gain falls to exactly 1
Frequency is the one point where the phase condition is met

bank.q: Define gain margin and phase margin. How are they read from a Bode plot, and what values are normally considered safe?
outline: Magnitude plot in dB, phase plot in degrees, both against log frequency
Gain crossover frequency where |Aβ| = 0 dB
PM = 180° − |phase at gain crossover|
GM = −|Aβ| in dB at the frequency where phase = −180°
Positive GM in dB and positive PM mean stable
Typical targets: PM of 45° to 60°, GM of 10 dB to 20 dB

bank.q: Explain the piezoelectric effect in quartz. Why does a crystal oscillator hold its frequency so well, and what is the difference between its series and parallel resonant frequencies?
outline: Quartz converts strain to charge and charge to strain
Equivalent circuit: series R_s, L_s, C_s in parallel with C_p
Very large L_s and very small C_s give Q in the tens of thousands
Series resonance where L_s and C_s cancel; parallel resonance slightly higher where C_p also takes part
High Q means the phase changes fast with frequency, so f₀ barely moves
Stability of a few parts per million over temperature

bank.q: Design an RC phase-shift oscillator using a BJT amplifier for an output of 1 kHz. Choose suitable R and C values, state the required amplifier gain, and list the component tolerances that matter.
outline: f₀ = 1/(2πRC√6) for three identical RC sections
Phase condition: 180° from the RC chain plus 180° from the CE amplifier
Choose C = 10 nF and solve for R ≈ 6.5 kΩ for 1 kHz
Magnitude condition: amplifier gain ≥ 29 (attenuation of the RC chain is 1/29)
Amplitude limiting needed, since gain drifts with temperature
Comment on tolerance of C and R and on loading of the network by the amplifier

bank.q: A Wien bridge oscillator is to run at 5 kHz using an op-amp. Find R for C = 10 nF, and find the feedback resistors that give the required gain. Explain how amplitude is stabilised.
outline: f₀ = 1/(2πRC) for the lead-lag network
R ≈ 3.2 kΩ for C = 10 nF at 5 kHz
Zero phase shift at f₀; the bridge is balanced in phase there
Required non-inverting gain = 3, so R_f/R₁ = 2
Slight excess gain starts oscillation
Thermistor or small lamp in the R₁ arm, or diode clipping, holds amplitude; gain falls as amplitude rises

bank.q: A Hartley oscillator uses L₁ = 100 µH, L₂ = 10 µH (no mutual inductance) and C = 250 pF. Calculate f₀ and the minimum amplifier gain needed to sustain oscillation.
outline: L_eq = L₁ + L₂ = 110 µH
f₀ = 1/(2π√(L_eq C))
Substitute to get f₀ ≈ 960 kHz; show the working with units
Feedback fraction β = L₁/(L₁ + L₂) if the feedback is taken across L₁
Minimum gain A = 1/β = (L₁ + L₂)/L₁ = 1.1
Practical gain is kept a little higher, with a nonlinearity to limit amplitude

bank.q: An amplifier has open-loop gain A = 10⁵, open-loop bandwidth 100 Hz and a feedback factor β = 0.01. Find the loop gain, the closed-loop gain and the new bandwidth. What happens to distortion?
outline: Bandwidth becomes 100 Hz × 1001 ≈ 100 kHz
Gain-bandwidth product roughly unchanged
Distortion and internal noise fall by about (1+Aβ)
Comment that the closed-loop gain now follows β, i.e. the resistors, not the transistor

bank.q: Design a Colpitts oscillator for 1 MHz using an inductor of 200 µH. Choose C₁ and C₂, state the feedback fraction, and give the gain condition. Why is the Clapp circuit preferred when a small tuning range is needed?
outline: C_eq from f₀ = 1/(2π√(L C_eq)); C_eq ≈ 127 pF
Choose C₁ and C₂ so that the series combination equals C_eq
Feedback fraction from the capacitive divider across C₁
Minimum gain A = 1/β
Clapp adds C₃ in series with L, so f₀ ≈ 1/(2π√(L C₃)) and transistor capacitance has little effect
Clapp gives better stability and easier tuning of a narrow band

bank.q: A three-stage amplifier has a loop gain whose magnitude is 0 dB at 100 kHz while the loop phase there is −150°, and whose phase reaches −180° at 1 MHz where the magnitude is −30 dB. Find the phase margin and gain margin and comment on stability.
outline: GM = 30 dB at the −180° crossing
Stable, because the magnitude is below 1 before the phase reaches −180°
PM of 30° is small; expect ringing and overshoot in the step response
Aim to raise PM towards 45°–60° by moving the dominant pole or adding compensation
Gain margin is comfortable, so instability would come from phase, not magnitude

bank.q: Compare the four feedback topologies for input resistance, output resistance and typical use. For a sensor with a high source resistance driving a low-resistance load, which topology would you choose and why?
outline: Voltage-series raises R_in and lowers R_out
Voltage-shunt lowers R_in and lowers R_out
Current-series raises R_in and raises R_out
Current-shunt lowers R_in and raises R_out
High source resistance needs a large R_in, so use series mixing
Low load resistance needs a small R_out, so use voltage sampling
Choice: voltage-series feedback; note the cost in gain and in stability margins

bank.q: Compare an RC phase-shift oscillator, a Wien bridge oscillator, a Colpitts oscillator and a crystal oscillator for frequency stability, tuning range and typical application. Which one would you pick for a fixed 10 MHz clock and why?
outline: RC phase shift: audio range, simple, poor stability, needs gain of about 29
Wien bridge: audio range, low distortion, gain of 3, stability limited by RC components
Colpitts or Hartley LC: radio range, tunable, moderate stability, needs a tapped tank
Crystal: fixed frequency, stability of parts per million, high Q, narrow tuning
For a fixed 10 MHz clock choose a crystal oscillator in a Colpitts-like circuit
Mention that crystals can be pulled only over a very small range, which is a feature for a clock

bank.q: Explain how negative feedback affects the poles of an amplifier and how this decides stability. Describe pole splitting and its cost.
outline: Transfer function with poles p₁, p₂; feedback moves them in the complex plane
Aβ is a complex number, so the −180° phase shift comes from the poles
As Aβ grows the poles move together, then break away and turn towards the imaginary axis
At the value where a pole pair crosses into the right half plane the circuit oscillates
Dominant-pole compensation pushes one pole low so the gain reaches 0 dB while the phase is far from −180°
Cost: reduced bandwidth and reduced slew rate

glossary.def: Returning a fraction of the output so that it subtracts from the input signal.
The ratio β = feedback signal ÷ output signal, a number with no unit.
The product Aβ, the total gain a signal sees in going round the amplifier and the feedback path once.
The gain with feedback connected, A/(1+Aβ) for negative feedback and A/(1−Aβ) for positive feedback.
The quantity (1+Aβ) by which gain is divided and stability of gain against device changes is multiplied.
The resistance seen looking into the amplifier input; raised by series mixing and lowered by shunt mixing.
The resistance seen looking back into the output; lowered by voltage sampling and raised by current sampling.
Output voltage sampled and feedback mixed in series at the input; high input resistance and low output resistance.
Output current sampled and feedback mixed in shunt at the input; low input resistance and high output resistance.
Two graphs of 20 log₁₀|Aβ| in dB and phase in degrees, both plotted against log frequency.
The lowest-frequency pole of the amplifier, which sets where the gain starts to fall at 20 dB per decade.
How many dB the loop gain could still rise before the circuit becomes unstable at the −180° phase point.
How many degrees of extra phase lag the loop can take at the 0 dB point before it oscillates.
The pair of conditions (loop magnitude 1 and loop phase a multiple of 360°) that allows steady oscillation.
An amplifier with positive feedback that produces a steady sine wave without any external input signal.
Any nonlinearity or gain-changing element that stops the oscillation growing and holds the loop gain at 1.
An oscillator using a series RC and a parallel RC arm to give zero phase shift at f₀ = 1/(2πRC).
An oscillator in which three RC sections produce 180° of phase shift at the oscillating frequency.
An inductor and capacitor connected together, storing energy at f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)).
An LC oscillator whose feedback comes from a tap on the inductor.
An LC oscillator whose feedback comes from a tap on a capacitive divider.
A Colpitts oscillator with a small extra capacitor in series with the inductor, giving improved frequency stability.
The property of certain crystals to produce a voltage when strained and to strain when a voltage is applied.
An oscillator whose frequency is set by a vibrating quartz plate of very high Q.
